prompt: Some cities offer free public transportation. Write an essay arguing whether more cities should do this.
text:
# Should More Cities Make Public Transit Free?

Free public transportation is an appealing idea. Buses and trains would be open to everyone, with no fares, no payment machines and no cost barrier. But a policy that sounds fair and green deserves a close look at what it costs and what it delivers. My view is that most cities should not make all transit free. They should instead target free or deeply discounted fares at the people who need them, and put the savings into better service.

The case for free transit starts with fairness. Low-income households spend a larger share of their money on getting around, and a fare can decide whether someone reaches a job interview, a clinic or a school. Removing fares helps those riders directly. It also simplifies things. Cities spend money on ticket machines, fare inspectors and payment systems, and in some systems these costs eat up a large part of what fares bring in. Boarding gets faster too, because no one has to wait at the front door while a rider pays.

Supporters also point to the environment and to traffic. If transit costs nothing, some drivers may leave their cars at home, which would mean fewer emissions and less congestion. Tallinn, Estonia, offers free rides to residents, and Luxembourg made transit free nationwide in 2020. Dozens of smaller cities, such as Dunkirk in France, have tried it as well.

The evidence on the environment is weaker than the pitch. Studies of free-fare programs often find that ridership rises, but much of the new ridership comes from people who would have walked or cycled, not from drivers. A short trip that once took a bike now takes a bus. That is a gain in convenience, but it does little for emissions and may crowd buses that people with no other option depend on. Drivers tend to respond more to the speed and reliability of a bus than to its price. If a bus is slow, infrequent or stuck in traffic, a free ticket will not persuade someone with a car to use it.

Money is the larger problem. Fares cover a meaningful part of operating costs in many cities, and in some large systems they cover a third or more. Eliminating them means the city must replace that income from taxes or cut something else. When transit budgets are tight, the usual result is worse service: fewer buses, longer waits and slower repairs. That harms the very riders free fares were meant to help. A free bus that comes every forty minutes is not much of a benefit to someone who needs to be at work on time.

A better approach uses the same goals with sharper tools. Cities can offer free or reduced fares to low-income residents, students, seniors and people with disabilities. Several cities already do this, and it directs public money to those who gain the most. They can also cap fares so that frequent riders never pay more than a set amount each week or month. Money saved from not subsidizing riders who can easily pay can go toward what actually draws people out of cars: frequent service, dedicated bus lanes and safe, clean stations.

There are cases where full free fares make sense. Small cities with low fare revenue and low costs for collecting it have less to lose. Free fares can also work for a limited time or on a single route, such as a downtown shuttle, or as a pilot to test demand. Cities that try it should measure results honestly, tracking who the new riders are and what trips they replaced.

In the end, the question is what a city wants transit to do. If the goal is to help people who struggle to afford fares, targeted discounts do that at lower cost. If the goal is to reduce driving, better service does more than a lower price. Free transit is a good slogan, but most cities will get more from spending the same money on buses that come often and arrive on time.
